cards.front: Primary visual cortex (V1) is also called {{c1::striate}} cortex, after a pale band of myelinated fibres visible to the naked eye.
cards.quote: Striate means striped: a pale band of myelinated fibres runs through it, visible to the naked eye.
cards.section: Two puzzles and one rule

cards.front: What is a visual neuron's receptive field?
cards.back: The patch of the visual field where a stimulus changes the neuron's firing.
cards.quote: A neuron's receptive field is the patch of the visual field where a stimulus changes its firing.
cards.section: Two puzzles and one rule

cards.front: State the approximate summation rule for retinal ganglion cells, LGN cells and V1 simple cells.
cards.back: The cell adds up the light falling on its receptive field, plus on ON regions and minus on OFF regions. A bigger sum means stronger drive, which the cell turns into firing through a threshold.
cards.why: It is a first approximation for steady light against a fixed background; it does not explain complex cells.
cards.quote: a good first approximation is that the cell adds up the light falling on its receptive field: plus on ON regions, minus on OFF regions.
cards.section: Two puzzles and one rule

cards.front: Under the summation rule, a visual neuron with spontaneous firing sees one stimulus whose sum is near zero and another whose sum is negative. Predict its firing for each.
cards.back: Near-zero sum: firing stays at the spontaneous rate. Negative sum: firing falls below the spontaneous rate, at most down to zero.
cards.why: Only a positive sum that clears the threshold raises firing; a negative sum lowers whatever firing there is.
cards.quote: a negative sum lowers whatever firing there is, down to zero.
cards.section: Two puzzles and one rule

cards.front: Because the lens inverts the image, where on the retina do the temporal visual field and the upper visual field fall?
cards.back: The temporal field falls on the nasal retina, and the upper field on the lower retina.
cards.quote: The lens inverts the image, so the temporal field falls on the nasal retina and the upper field on the lower retina.
cards.section: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world

cards.front: At the optic chiasm of humans and other primates, only the fibres from the {{c1::nasal}} half of each retina cross to the other side.
cards.back: Temporal-retina fibres stay ipsilateral.
cards.quote: only the fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross to the other side.
cards.section: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world

cards.front: In primates, what part of the visual world does each optic tract carry, and from which eyes?
cards.back: The contralateral visual hemifield, from both eyes. The left tract carries everything to the right of the point of gaze.
cards.quote: Behind the chiasm, each optic tract carries the contralateral (opposite) visual hemifield from both eyes
cards.section: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world

cards.front: In a human, consider the fibres from the temporal half of the right retina. Which half of the visual world do they report, and which optic tract do they join?
cards.back: The left half of the world (the right eye's nasal field). They do not cross at the chiasm, so they join the right optic tract.
cards.why: The lens inverts the image, so the nasal field falls on the temporal retina; only nasal-retina fibres cross.
cards.quote: The right eye's temporal-retina fibres, which see its nasal (left) field, stayed on their own side and joined it too.
cards.section: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world

cards.front: Where does the optic tract mainly end, and how does that relay handle the two eyes' inputs?
cards.back: In the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, which keeps the two eyes' inputs in separate layers.
cards.quote: The tract ends mainly in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, a relay that keeps the two eyes' inputs in separate layers.
cards.section: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world

cards.front: How do the optic radiations for the upper and lower visual field differ in route and in where they end in V1?
cards.back: Upper-field fibres sweep forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) and end below the calcarine sulcus. Lower-field fibres run through the parietal lobe and end above it.
cards.quote: Fibres for the upper field sweep forward through the temporal lobe in Meyer's loop and end below the calcarine sulcus
cards.section: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world

cards.front: A lesion destroys the centre of the optic chiasm and nothing else. Predict the visual-field defect and explain it.
cards.back: Both temporal fields are lost, a bitemporal hemianopia.
cards.why: The crossing fibres come from the nasal retina of each eye, and the nasal retina sees the temporal field.
cards.quote: Chiasm, centre: the crossing nasal fibres of both eyes are cut, so both temporal fields are lost.
cards.section: Four defects

cards.front: Complete interruption of the optic tract, the entire optic radiation or the entire V1 representation on one side causes a {{c1::homonymous hemianopia}}: loss of the opposite half of the field in both eyes. Partial lesions give partial defects.
cards.quote: Optic tract, radiation or V1 on one side: the opposite half of the field in both eyes
cards.section: Four defects

cards.front: The right optic nerve is cut completely, in front of the chiasm. Predict the visual-field defect in each eye.
cards.back: The whole field of the right eye is lost; the left eye's field is intact.
cards.why: Before the chiasm the nerve carries every fibre from one eye and no fibres from the other.
cards.quote: Optic nerve: loss of the whole field of the eye on the same side.
cards.section: Four defects

cards.front: A lesion completely interrupts the parietal branch of the left optic radiation, sparing Meyer's loop. Predict the visual-field defect.
cards.back: Loss of the lower right quarter of the field in both eyes, a quadrantanopia.
cards.why: The left radiation carries the right hemifield, and its parietal branch carries the lower field.
cards.quote: Meyer's loop damage gives an upper quarter defect on the opposite side, reported after temporal-lobe surgery; parietal radiation damage gives a lower quarter.
cards.section: Four defects

cards.front: What are incongruous defects and macular sparing, and which lesions of the visual pathway tend to show each?
cards.back: Incongruous: the losses in the two eyes do not match closely, often after tract lesions. Macular sparing: central vision is spared, often after V1 lesions. Both are tendencies only.
cards.quote: Tract lesions often give incongruous defects, meaning the losses in the two eyes do not match closely, and V1 lesions often spare central vision, called macular sparing.
cards.section: Where the defect descriptions come from

cards.front: A patient loses the upper right quarter of the visual field in both eyes. Where could a single lesion be?
cards.back: In left Meyer's loop, or in the cortex below the left calcarine sulcus.
cards.why: The upper right field falls on the lower left quarter of each retina; those fibres join the left tract and run as upper-field fibres through left Meyer's loop.
cards.quote: Upper-field fibres run in left Meyer's loop to the cortex below the left calcarine sulcus, so either site fits.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A patient has lost the right half of the field in both eyes. Can the field test alone tell a left optic tract lesion from a left V1 lesion? What features might hint at one or the other?
cards.back: Not with certainty: a lesion of the left tract, LGN, radiation or V1 all remove the right hemifield of both eyes. Poorly matched losses lean toward the tract; spared central vision leans toward V1.
cards.why: Rests on each tract carrying the contralateral hemifield, plus incongruity and macular sparing being tendencies only.
cards.quote: Those fibres join in the left optic tract, so the lesion is in the left tract, left LGN, left optic radiation or left V1.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Rank three stimuli for an ON-centre retinal ganglion cell: a small spot filling the centre, diffuse light over the whole field, and light on the surround only.
cards.back: Central spot strongest; diffuse light weak; surround-only light drops firing below the spontaneous rate.
cards.why: The spot lands only on plus. Diffuse light lands on plus and minus, which largely cancel. Surround light lands only on minus.
cards.quote: Diffuse light lands on plus and minus together, and they largely cancel, so the response is weak.
cards.section: What: adding up the light

cards.front: Hubel and Wiesel recorded extracellularly from single cells in anaesthetized cat visual cortex while projecting spots, slits and bars onto a screen. What did they observe about spots versus bars?
cards.back: Spots often did little, while a slit or bar at the right angle drove some cells hard.
cards.quote: Spots often did little; a slit or bar at the right angle drove some cells hard.
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: Describe the receptive field of a V1 simple cell.
cards.back: Separate ON and OFF subregions that are long, narrow and side by side; a common layout is a narrow ON strip with an OFF strip on each side.
cards.quote: The subregions are long and narrow and lie side by side. A common layout is a narrow ON strip with an OFF strip on each side.
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: A made-up simple cell's field is a grid six squares tall: a centre column of six ON squares (+1 each) flanked on each side by six OFF squares (−0.5 each). It has no spontaneous firing; rate = sum − 2 when the sum exceeds 2, otherwise 0. Find the rate for a bar along the ON strip and for the same bar turned to lie across the field.
cards.back: Along the ON strip: sum = 6 × (+1) = +6, rate = 6 − 2 = 4. Across the field: +1 − 0.5 − 0.5 = 0, rate = 0.
cards.why: Turning the bar moves it off the ON strip onto the OFF flanks, so the sum collapses.
cards.quote: its rate is the sum minus 2 when the sum is above 2, and zero otherwise (arbitrary units).
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: Same made-up simple cell (six ON squares at +1 flanked by two columns of six OFF squares at −0.5; rate = sum − 2 above a threshold of 2). Find the rate for (a) a bar covering only three squares of the ON strip, and (b) a wide bar covering the whole ON strip plus one whole OFF strip.
cards.back: (a) Sum = +3, rate = 3 − 2 = 1. (b) Sum = +6 − 3 = +3, rate = 1. Both are far weaker than the aligned full bar (rate 4).
cards.why: Shortening the bar loses plus; widening it adds minus.
cards.quote: a centre column of six ON squares, each worth +1, with a column of six OFF squares on each side, each worth −0.5.
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: Under the summation rule, why is a simple cell's orientation selectivity not a separate property added on top of its receptive field?
cards.back: To a first approximation it comes from the field's shape: turning the bar takes it off the ON strip and onto the OFF flanks, so the sum falls.
cards.quote: Turning the bar takes it off the ON strip and onto the OFF flanks, and the sum falls.
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: A simple cell's ON and OFF subregions are made longer while their width stays the same. Predict the effect on orientation tuning.
cards.back: Tuning becomes sharper.
cards.why: As the bar turns, a longer strip loses ON coverage and gains OFF coverage faster, so the sum falls faster. Length relative to width is what counts.
cards.quote: Make the subregions longer while keeping their width, and the sum falls faster as the bar turns, so the cell is more sharply tuned
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: How does a simple cell's spike threshold shape its measured orientation tuning?
cards.back: Only the part of the sum above threshold makes spikes, so spike tuning is narrower than the field's sum alone predicts. Without the threshold, the rule predicts tuning that is too broad.
cards.quote: so measured spike tuning is narrower than the field's sum alone predicts
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: In the made-up simple cell (six ON squares at +1, two flanking OFF columns at −0.5), a manipulation lowers the threshold from 2 to 0, so rate = sum whenever the sum is positive. Predict the effect on its responses and on its orientation tuning.
cards.back: A single-square spot now fires (rate 1 instead of 0), the aligned bar rises from 4 to 6, and partly turned bars with small positive sums now fire. Spike tuning becomes broader.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that only the part of the sum above threshold makes spikes.
cards.quote: applied without the threshold, the rule predicts tuning that is too broad.
cards.section: Why a bar beats a spot

cards.front: How did Hubel and Wiesel propose that a simple cell's elongated field is built, and what was the status of that proposal?
cards.back: Several LGN cells with ON centres in a row all excite one cortical cell, giving an ON strip; their surrounds and aligned OFF-centre cells add OFF flanks. It was a proposal; 1990s recordings supported the aligned-input step.
cards.quote: If several LGN cells whose ON centres lie in a row all excite one cortical cell, that cell gets an elongated ON strip.
cards.section: How might such a field be built?

cards.front: A made-up V1 cell has a spontaneous rate of 4 spikes/s. Mean rates: 0 degrees, 6; 30 degrees, 20; 60 degrees, 44; 90 degrees, 18; 120 degrees, 6; 150 degrees, 4 spikes/s. Assuming linear change between samples and measuring half height from the spontaneous rate, estimate the full width at half height.
cards.why: Measuring from the spontaneous rate makes the width describe the stimulus-driven response.
cards.quote: Note the two baselines: Step 2 measured from the spontaneous rate, so the width describes the stimulus-driven response, while Step 5 uses raw rates.
cards.section: Reading a tuning curve

cards.front: The same made-up V1 cell prefers 60 degrees (44 spikes/s); at 150 degrees it fires 4 spikes/s, equal to its spontaneous rate. Compute the orientation index (R_pref − R_orth)/(R_pref + R_orth) with raw rates, then with the spontaneous rate subtracted from both.
cards.why: R_orth is 90 degrees from the preferred orientation. An index near 1 shows strong preference but does not give tuning width. State which baseline you use.
cards.quote: With the spontaneous rate subtracted from both rates, the index here would be 1.00, because the orthogonal response equals the spontaneous rate.
cards.section: Reading a tuning curve

cards.front: Why can no cell that computes a single sum over its receptive field be excited by both a bright bar and a dark bar at the same place?
cards.back: Reversing the contrast flips the sign of the sum, so if one bar gives a positive sum the other gives a negative one.
cards.quote: no single sum can be excited by both a bright and a dark bar at the same place, because reversing the contrast flips the sign of the sum.
cards.section: Beyond one sum: complex cells

cards.front: How do complex cells in cat V1 differ from simple cells in their responses to a bar?
cards.back: A correctly oriented bar drives a complex cell over much of its field, while a wrongly oriented bar still does little. Complex cells keep orientation tuning but tolerate position.
cards.quote: A bar at the wrong angle still did little, so they do not ignore orientation; they tolerate position.
cards.section: Beyond one sum: complex cells

cards.front: What wiring did Hubel and Wiesel propose to explain complex cells?
cards.back: Several simple cells with the same preferred orientation but fields at slightly different positions all excite one complex cell. It was a proposal, and how far every complex cell follows it is debated.
cards.why: In the proposed pooling scheme, where the inputs' excitatory responses overlap enough, at least one responds strongly as the bar shifts, so orientation is kept and position is tolerated. Responses weaken at gaps and at the edges of the covered span.
cards.quote: Several simple cells share one orientation but have fields at slightly different positions, and all of them excite one complex cell.
cards.section: Beyond one sum: complex cells

cards.front: A V1 cell responds equally to a bright bar and a dark bar of the same orientation at the same position. Could the single-sum rule explain it? What kind of computation could?
cards.back: No; a single sum flips sign when contrast reverses. It needs a nonlinearity beyond one sum, such as squaring and adding two quadrature filters (energy model, E = u² + v²), where reversing contrast flips u and v but leaves E unchanged.
cards.why: Rests on the sign-flip rule plus the energy model; adding the filters without squaring would be just another sum.
cards.quote: Reversing the contrast flips the sign of u and v and leaves E unchanged.
cards.section: Complex cells as pooled pairs

cards.front: V1 is {{c1::retinotopic}}: neighbouring points in the visual field excite neighbouring points in cortex.
cards.quote: V1 is retinotopic: neighbouring points in the visual field excite neighbouring points in cortex
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: What is cortical magnification, and why is it largest at the fovea?
cards.back: The millimetres of cortex given to one degree of visual field. It is largest at the fovea largely because more ganglion cells serve each degree there, and it falls steeply with eccentricity.
cards.quote: It is largest at the fovea, largely because more ganglion cells serve each degree there, so more cortex is needed to map them.
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: Near the macaque fovea, assume a locally constant cortical magnification of 15 mm per degree. Two active spots on V1 lie 4.5 mm apart. How far apart are the stimuli in the visual field?
cards.back: Separation = distance ÷ M = 4.5 mm ÷ 15 mm/degree = 0.30 degrees.
cards.why: Valid only near the fovea; magnification falls steeply with eccentricity, so one value cannot be used across the field.
cards.quote: Because magnification falls steeply with eccentricity, this holds only near the fovea; never apply one value across the field.
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: A human V1 simple cell responds best to a vertical bar in the upper left quarter of the visual field. Which hemisphere and which side of the calcarine sulcus hold it, and what sets its preference for vertical?
cards.back: Right V1, below the calcarine sulcus, reached through right Meyer's loop. Its preference comes from the vertical layout of its ON and OFF subregions.
cards.why: Where the field sits follows the pathway (contralateral hemifield, upper field below the sulcus); the plus and minus layout sets the best stimulus.
cards.quote: Where the patch sits tells you which part of the world the cell reports.
cards.section: Two puzzles and one rule

cards.front: What is a cortical column in V1?
cards.back: A group of cells, running through the thickness of the cortex, that share a property such as orientation preference or eye preference.
cards.quote: On top of the map sit columns: groups of cells, running through the thickness of the cortex, that share a property.
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: Hubel and Wiesel (1968) mapped orientation columns and ocular-dominance columns along the same penetrations in monkey V1. What did they report about the two sets of boundaries, and what did later optical imaging find?
cards.back: The boundaries seemed independent of each other. Later imaging found the maps systematically related: pinwheel centres tend to lie near the middle of ocular-dominance columns.
cards.quote: They reported boundaries that seemed to be independent of each other; later work found the two maps related (see Going deeper).
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: In rat V1, orientation-tuned neighbours prefer unrelated orientations, a layout called {{c1::salt-and-pepper}}.
cards.quote: neighbours preferred unrelated orientations, a layout called salt-and-pepper.
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: Two-photon calcium imaging of rat V1 finds sharply orientation-tuned cells with no local orientation map. Why does imaging cat area 18 with the same method matter, and what two conclusions follow?
cards.back: In cat area 18 the method resolved maps with borders one or two cells wide, so the rat result is not a method too coarse to see a map. Conclusions: tuning does not need a map, and columns are not universal.
cards.why: A positive control rules out a technical explanation for a negative result.
cards.quote: The same method was not blind to maps: in cat area 18, preferences were so orderly that direction-column borders were one or two cells wide.
cards.section: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns

cards.front: In monkeys, inferior temporal lesions impaired object discrimination and posterior parietal lesions impaired a spatial landmark task. What two streams were proposed from this evidence?
cards.back: A ventral (occipitotemporal) stream for object vision, "what", and a dorsal (occipitoparietal) stream for spatial vision, "where"; a working hypothesis.
cards.quote: Inferior temporal lesions impaired object discrimination; posterior parietal lesions impaired a landmark task that depends on spatial position.
cards.section: Beyond V1: two streams

cards.front: Patient D.F., who has visual form agnosia, matches the width of plaques poorly, yet when she reaches to pick them up her grip opens in proportion to width. What does this dissociation suggest?
cards.back: Visual information that guides action is spared while perceptual report fails, supporting the proposal that the ventral stream serves perception and the dorsal stream the visual control of action.
cards.why: Her damage lies mainly in ventral lateral occipital cortex on both sides; dorsal areas still responded during grasping.
cards.quote: Her width matching was poor, yet when she reached to pick the same plaques up, her grip opened in proportion to width.
cards.section: Beyond V1: two streams

cards.front: Give two limits on using patient D.F. to support the perception-action account of the two visual streams.
cards.back: She is one patient, and one dissociation does not localize a circuit. Also, her report and grasp tasks differ in movement and feedback, and the streams are densely interconnected.
cards.quote: D.F. is one patient, and one dissociation does not localize a circuit.
cards.section: Beyond V1: two streams

cards.front: Under the perception-action account of the two visual streams, predict the pattern for a patient whose dorsal stream is damaged but whose ventral stream is intact, tested on the same width-matching and grasping tasks as D.F.
cards.back: The reverse of D.F.: width matching relatively spared, but grip scaling during the reach impaired.
cards.why: Rests on the account's claim that the ventral stream serves perception and the dorsal stream the visual control of action; a single case would still not localize a circuit.
cards.quote: Goodale and Milner proposed in 1992 that the ventral stream serves perception and the dorsal stream the visual control of action.
cards.section: Beyond V1: two streams

cards.front: Besides the LGN, name targets of retinal axons in the optic tract or at the chiasm.
cards.back: The superior colliculus and the pretectum, and, via a small set of axons leaving at the chiasm, the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
cards.quote: a small set of retinal axons leaves at the chiasm for the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
cards.section: Other targets of the optic tract
